chunks.title: Retinal circulation
chunks.tldr: CRA = end artery. Retinal capillaries feed the inner 2/3; choriocapillaris feeds the outer 1/3. Capillary endothelium tight junctions = inner blood–retinal barrier. Pericytes autoregulate.
points: Central retinal artery enters the optic nerve ~1 cm behind the globe. Arterioles have a discontinuous internal elastic lamina.
Two capillary plexuses: inner (ganglion cell layer) and outer (inner nuclear layer).
Capillary-free zones around arterioles and at the fovea (FAZ).
Capillaries: endothelial cells (tight junctions), basement membrane, pericytes (contractile). No muscle/elastic.
Veins: little muscle, distensible.
chunks.hook: Inner 2/3 = retinal vessels. Outer 1/3 = choroid.

cards.q: Which cells form the inner blood–retinal barrier?
Which part of the retina does the choriocapillaris supply?

chunks.title: DR: who's at risk
chunks.tldr: Biggest risk = duration (type 1: 50% at 10 years, 90% at 30). Others: poor control (HbA1c), BP, pregnancy, nephropathy, lipids. DMO = commonest cause of vision loss.
points: ~40% of diabetics have DR; sight-threatening up to 10%; PDR 5–10%.
Rare in the first 5 years or before puberty, but ~5% of type 2 have DR at diagnosis.
DCCT/UKPDS: tight glucose control prevents/slows DR. HbA1c target 6–7% (8% frail). Each 1% drop → ~1/3 fewer microvascular complications.
Sudden tight control can briefly worsen DR.
Pregnancy: worse if DR/poor control before, rapid tightening, pre-eclampsia. ~5% of mild and 1/3 of moderate NPDR → PDR. DMO late in pregnancy often resolves after.
BP <140/80 (esp. type 2 with maculopathy).
Nephropathy worsens DR; kidney transplant can improve it.
Also: lipids, smoking, cataract surgery, obesity, anaemia.
Other diabetic eye problems: unstable refraction, iris transillumination, styes, xanthelasma, early cataract, NVG, CN palsies, reduced corneal sensation, papillopathy, Wolfram, mucormycosis.
chunks.hook: DR risk = Time + Sugar + Pressure.

cards.q: Strongest risk factor for diabetic retinopathy?
Proportion of type 1 diabetics with DR after 30 years?

chunks.title: DR signs: the building blocks
chunks.tldr: Microaneurysms (first sign) → dot/blot & flame haemorrhages → exudates (leaky) → cotton-wool spots, venous beading, IRMA, deep blots (ischaemia) → NVD/NVE.
points: Microaneurysms: capillary outpouchings where pericytes are lost; often temporal to the fovea. FA: tiny bright dots (more than you see), leak late.
Flame haemorrhages: nerve fibre layer (superficial arterioles).
Dot/blot: middle layers (venous end of capillaries).
Deep dark round blots: haemorrhagic infarcts → marker of PDR risk.
Exudates: yellow lipid/macrophages in the outer plexiform layer, at the edge of oedema, rings (circinate) around leaky microaneurysms. Clear slowly when leakage stops.
Cotton-wool spots: swollen axon ends (cytoid bodies) from ischaemia; FA dark.
Venous changes: dilatation, looping, beading, sausage segments → extent predicts PDR.
IRMA: shunts from arterioles to venules next to non-perfused areas; don't leak on FA (NV do).
Arterial: narrowing, silver wiring in severe ischaemia.
PDR needs >¼ of retina non-perfused. NVD = on/within 1 DD of the disc. NVE elsewhere. NVI (rubeosis) → NVG. FA: NV leak heavily.
chunks.hook: IRMA stays put (no leak). New vessels leak like crazy.

cards.q: Earliest clinical sign of diabetic retinopathy?
How do IRMA and NVE differ on FA?
cards.a: IRMA don't leak; new vessels leak profusely.

cards.q: In which retinal layer are hard exudates mainly located?

chunks.title: ETDRS grading & the 4-2-1 rule
chunks.tldr: Severe NPDR = 4-2-1: severe haemorrhages in 4 quadrants, venous beading in 2, IRMA in 1. High-risk PDR: NVD ≥⅓ disc area, any NVD + VH, or NVE ≥½ DA + VH.
points: No DR → review 12 months.
Very mild NPDR: microaneurysms only.
Mild NPDR: MAs, haemorrhages, exudates, CWS; no IRMA or significant beading. Review 6–12 months.
Moderate NPDR: severe haemorrhages in 1–3 quadrants or mild IRMA; beading ≤1 quadrant. ~6 months (PDR in up to 26% in a year).
Severe NPDR (4-2-1): any one → review 4 months (PDR up to 50% in a year).
Very severe NPDR: two or more of 4-2-1 → 2–3 months (high-risk PDR up to 45%).
PDR (mild–moderate): NV not meeting high-risk → consider treatment.
High-risk PDR: NVD >⅓ DA, any NVD with VH, NVE >½ DA with VH → treat now (same day if symptomatic).
Clinical words: background (MAs, haemorrhages, exudates), maculopathy, pre-proliferative (CWS, venous changes, IRMA, deep blots), proliferative, advanced (TRD, persistent VH, NVG).
chunks.hook: 4-2-1: four quadrants bleed, two bead, one has IRMA.

cards.q: State the 4-2-1 rule.
cards.a: Severe haemorrhages in 4 quadrants, venous beading in 2, or IRMA in 1 = severe NPDR.

cards.q: Name one high-risk PDR criterion.
cards.a: NVD >⅓ disc area; any NVD with vitreous haemorrhage; NVE >½ disc area with vitreous haemorrhage.

chunks.title: Diabetic maculopathy & CSMO
chunks.tldr: Types: focal (exudate rings, FA focal leak), diffuse (thickening, CMO), ischaemic (looks OK, bad VA, big FAZ on FA). CSMO = thickening or exudates (with thickening) within 500 µm of the centre, or ≥1 DA thickening within 1 DD.
points: Commonest cause of vision loss in diabetes (esp. type 2).
Focal: localised thickening + exudate rings; FA late focal leak; good perfusion.
Diffuse: widespread thickening ± cystoid spaces (OCT; FA flower-petal).
Ischaemic: macula may look normal but VA poor; FA shows enlarged/irregular FAZ → poor prognosis.
CSMO (ETDRS): (1) thickening within 500 µm of the centre; (2) exudates within 500 µm with adjacent thickening; (3) thickening ≥1 disc area any part within 1 disc diameter.
Today: classify as centre-involving vs not on OCT.
chunks.hook: 500 µm = the danger circle around the fovea.

cards.q: Key FA finding in ischaemic maculopathy?
One ETDRS criterion for CSMO?
cards.a: Retinal thickening within 500 µm of the macular centre.

chunks.title: Treating DMO
chunks.tldr: Centre-involving DMO → anti-VEGF (Protocol I). VA ≤6/15 → aflibercept best (Protocol T). Non-centre with threatening exudates → focal/grid laser. Pseudophakic or anti-VEGF not allowed → steroid implants.
points: General: education, glucose, BP, lipids, fenofibrate (type 2), stop smoking, treat anaemia/renal disease.
Protocol I: ranibizumab beats laser for centre-involving DMO; defer laser ≥6 months; good to 5 years with fewer injections.
Protocol T: VA better than 6/15 → aflibercept = bevacizumab = ranibizumab. VA 6/15 or worse → aflibercept better.
Good VA (≥6/7.5) with DMO: observation is reasonable.
Start: monthly × 3–6, then as-needed. Improvement after 3 injections predicts long-term response.
Focal laser: 50–100 µm, 0.05–0.1 s, light grey burns on leaking MAs 500–3000 µm from the foveola. Grid: mild burns on diffuse thickening, ≥500 µm from fovea and disc.
Subthreshold micropulse: no visible burn, can go subfoveal.
Intravitreal triamcinolone (pseudophakes, pregnancy, recent MI), dexamethasone implant (Ozurdex), fluocinolone implant (longer). Watch IOP, cataract.
Persistent after 6 months anti-VEGF → add laser or switch to Ozurdex.
PDR + DMO → anti-VEGF alone may cover both.
PPV if taut posterior hyaloid/VMT or ERM.
chunks.hook: Bad vision (≤6/15)? Aflibercept. Off-centre exudates creeping in? Laser.

cards.q: DRCR Protocol T: which agent is better when VA is 6/15 or worse?
Minimum distance from the foveola for conventional grid laser?

chunks.title: PRP & anti-VEGF for PDR
chunks.tldr: PRP is still the mainstay (DRS: severe NVD risk 26% → 9%). Protocol S: ranibizumab ≈ PRP at 5 years (less DMO, better field) if the patient will keep coming back. PRP: ~400 µm spots, 1–1.5 widths apart, outside the arcades, fractionated.
points: Consent: driving field loss possible, night/colour vision, risk to centre (DMO worsens; fractionate).
Protocol S / CLARITY: anti-VEGF as good as PRP; ~half get VH either way. Choose PRP if follow-up or cost is a worry.
DMO + PDR: anti-VEGF (± PRP). Non-centre CSMO: do macular laser before or with PRP.
Lens: panfundoscopic (spot ×2 → set 200 µm for 400 µm on retina) or Mainster/Area Centralis (≈1:1). Image inverted.
Duration 10–50 ms (modern), light burns, spacing 1–1.5 burn widths. Pattern scan multispot.
Amount: ~1500 burns first session; mild PDR 2500–3500, moderate ~4000, severe ~7000 total.
Pattern: barrier temporal to the macula first; spare 2 DD nasal to the disc; severe PDR → inferior first (blood settles there); avoid traction.
Review 4–6 weeks after completion.
Regression: blunted tips, shrinking NV → ghost vessels/fibrosis, less IRMA/venous change. Contraction can cause VH or TRD.
Targeted PRP: laser only non-perfused areas on wide-field FA.
chunks.hook: PRP rule: Fence the macula, start inferiorly, spare the disc's nasal side.

cards.q: Typical retinal burn size for PRP?
Why treat the inferior retina first in severe PDR?
cards.a: Vitreous haemorrhage settles inferiorly and could block later treatment.

cards.q: Protocol S conclusion?
cards.a: Intravitreal ranibizumab is as effective as PRP for PDR at 5 years.

chunks.title: Advanced diabetic eye disease & papillopathy
chunks.tldr: Advanced = VH, tractional RD, rubeosis/NVG. PPV for: non-clearing VH, TRD threatening the macula, combined TRD/RRD, dense premacular haemorrhage. Diabetic papillopathy = young diabetic, swollen hyperaemic disc, mild blur, recovers.
points: Haemorrhage: preretinal (retrohyaloid) or intragel; ochre membrane. B-scan to check retina.
TRD: fibrovascular contraction at vitreoretinal adhesions; incomplete PVD.
Rubeosis: severe ischaemia or failed surgery → NVG.

PPV indications: severe persistent VH (classically ~3 months; earlier now), macula-threatening TRD (urgent), combined TRD + RRD (urgent), dense premacular retrohyaloid haemorrhage (or YAG hyaloidotomy), anterior NV with media opacity. Extramacular TRD can be watched. Endolaser PRP during PPV.

Diabetic papillopathy: young diabetics, mild painless blur, often unilateral, hyperaemic disc swelling + surface telangiectasia (not NVD). Bilateral → exclude raised ICP. Resolves over months; 80% ≥6/12.
Non-diabetic retinopathy: DR-like spots in up to 10% of non-diabetics >40 → vascular risk, maybe pre-diabetes.
chunks.hook: Traction on the macula = operate now. Traction elsewhere = watch.

cards.q: Diabetic TRD not involving the macula: management?
Laser to disperse a premacular retrohyaloid haemorrhage?

chunks.title: RVO: risk factors & work-up
chunks.tldr: Biggest risks: age, hypertension, high lipids, diabetes, glaucoma/OHT (CRVO), OCP (young women). Work-up for all: BP, FBC, ESR, glucose, lipids, protein electrophoresis. Young/bilateral → thrombophilia screen.
points: Artery and vein share a sheath at crossings → hard artery squeezes the vein → clot.
Age (>50% over 65), hypertension (2/3 of over-50s; esp. BRVO), lipids (1/3), diabetes (up to 15%), glaucoma/OHT (CRVO), OCP, smoking.
Uncommon: dehydration, myeloma/polycythaemia, thrombophilia (homocysteine, antiphospholipid, factor V Leiden), periphlebitis (Behçet, sarcoid, GPA), orbital disease, renal failure.
All: BP, ESR/PV, FBC, glucose, cholesterol/HDL, plasma protein electrophoresis (± U&E, TFTs, ECG).
Selected (<50, bilateral, past/family thrombosis): CXR, CRP, homocysteine, thrombophilia screen (incl. anticardiolipin), autoantibodies, ACE, syphilis, carotid Doppler.
After RVO: control risk factors, stop smoking; stop OCP, avoid oestrogen HRT; aspirin only if systemic indication; avoid dehydration.
chunks.hook: RVO = Old, high Pressure, high fat. Young woman? Check the Pill.

cards.q: Commonest association of RVO in young women?
Ocular condition linked with higher CRVO risk?

chunks.title: Branch retinal vein occlusion
chunks.tldr: Usually superotemporal, at an AV crossing. Haemorrhages in one sector. Main vision threat = macular oedema → anti-VEGF (BRAVO, VIBRANT) or Ozurdex. NV (>5 DA non-perfusion) → sector laser.
points: Macula involved → sudden blur/distortion. Peripheral → may be silent.
Dilated tortuous vein segment, flame + dot/blot haemorrhages in its territory, CWS, oedema. Superotemporal commonest.
Resolves over 6–12 months → sheathed veins, collaterals (can cross the horizontal raphe; good sign).
NVE ~8% by 3 years (much higher if >5 disc areas non-perfused); NVE > NVD; usually 6–12 months. NVI/NVG only 2–3%.
FA: delayed filling, non-perfusion, leakage, collaterals.
Treat BP/lipids. Observe if VA ≥6/9.

Macular oedema: anti-VEGF early (BRAVO: ranibizumab beats grid laser; VIBRANT: aflibercept). Ozurdex (repeat 4–6 months; IOP/cataract). Grid laser (avoid within ½ DD of fovea, haemorrhages, collaterals) if VA ≤6/12 after 3–6 months with good perfusion. Micropulse. Triamcinolone.
NV: sector scatter laser (400–500 µm, 1 burn apart) to the ischaemic area ± anti-VEGF. NVI → urgent sector PRP.
Review 3 months, then 3–6-monthly for 2 years.
Prognosis: 50–60% keep >6/15 even untreated; ~¼ ≤6/60.
chunks.hook: BRVO = one sector bleeding, usually upper outer, at a crossing.

cards.q: Non-perfusion area predicting NV in BRVO?
Commonest cause of persistent poor vision after BRVO?

chunks.title: CRVO: non-ischaemic vs ischaemic
chunks.tldr: Ischaemic CRVO: VA <6/60, RAPD, lots of deep blots + CWS, FA >10 DA non-perfusion → NVI in ~50% at ~100 days. Non-ischaemic: milder, no/mild RAPD, but 1/3 convert.
points: Impending CRVO: younger, mild venous dilatation, few haemorrhages, blur on waking.

Non-ischaemic (commoner): sudden blur, mild haemorrhages in all quadrants, mild disc/macular oedema, perivenular ischaemic whitening (young), FAF fern-like pattern. FA: delayed transit, good perfusion. ~1/3 become ischaemic.
Vision: good start → good end; worse than 6/60 → ischaemia likely.
Ischaemic: VA usually CF or worse, RAPD, severe tortuosity, extensive deep blot/flame haemorrhages, many CWS, disc swelling.
NVI ~50%, typically 2–4 months ('100-day glaucoma'). Check pupil margin + undilated gonioscopy (angle NV can come first).
Retinal NV only ~5% (less than BRVO).
Disc collaterals (optociliary shunts) → lower NV risk.
FA: >10 DA non-perfusion = high NV risk. ERG depressed.
Late: macular atrophy, ERM, CMO.
Hemiretinal vein occlusion: superior or inferior half → altitudinal field defect; NVI risk between BRVO and CRVO; NVD more common. Manage like CRVO if ischaemic, otherwise like BRVO.
Papillophlebitis: young, disc swelling dominant, peripapillary haemorrhages, mild VA loss, good prognosis (bilateral → exclude raised ICP).
chunks.hook: Bad VA + RAPD + blood-and-thunder fundus = ischaemic CRVO → watch for 100-day glaucoma.

cards.q: FA threshold of non-perfusion suggesting high NV risk in CRVO?
Why do gonioscopy before dilating in ischaemic CRVO?
cards.a: Angle neovascularisation can occur without pupil-margin NV.

chunks.title: Treating CRVO complications
chunks.tldr: CMO (VA <6/9 or thick on OCT) → anti-VEGF (CRUISE, COPERNICUS) or Ozurdex (GENEVA). Laser doesn't help vision. NVI/angle NV → urgent PRP + anti-VEGF. No prophylactic PRP. Ischaemic → monthly review × 6 months.
points: Macular oedema: treat if VA worse than 6/9 and/or CST >250 µm; little benefit if ≤6/120.
CRUISE (ranibizumab), COPERNICUS (aflibercept, works PRN too), bevacizumab also used.
GENEVA: Ozurdex effect peaks ~2 months, gone by 6 → repeat. Better if within 90 days. COMRADE: ranibizumab beat dexamethasone at 6 months.
SCORE: triamcinolone 1 mg helped (IOP/cataract risk).
Grid laser: improves anatomy, not vision (except some young).
Experimental: chorioretinal anastomosis, radial optic neurotomy, rtPA.
NVI/angle NV: PRP now (1500–2000 burns initially, avoid haemorrhages, more later) + anti-VEGF 6-weekly until stable. NVG may be delayed up to 18 months → 3-monthly follow-up for 2–3 years.
Prophylactic PRP not supported by evidence.
VH: anti-VEGF or PPV + endolaser.
Review: ischaemic → monthly for 6 months, then 2–3 years. Non-ischaemic → 3 months, discharge ~18–24 months; return if worse vision, pain or redness.
chunks.hook: CMO → injections. NVI → laser + injections.

cards.q: Does macular grid laser improve vision in CRVO macular oedema?
cards.a: No (anatomy improves, vision doesn't, except in some younger patients).

cards.q: Is prophylactic PRP recommended in ischaemic CRVO?
cards.a: No; treat promptly when NVI/angle NV appears.

chunks.title: Retinal artery occlusion: causes & work-up
chunks.tldr: Mostly emboli from the carotid: Hollenhorst (shiny yellow cholesterol), fibrin-platelet (grey), calcific (white, from valves). Always ask about GCA in older patients. Urgent stroke work-up.
points: CRA = first branch of the ophthalmic artery (from ICA) → emboli go straight there.

Causes: atheroembolism/thrombosis, GCA, vasculitis (SLE, GPA, PAN), vasospasm (migraine), hypotension, cardiac (AF, valves, myxoma, endocarditis), thrombophilia (1/3 of young), sickle, Susac syndrome (BRAO + deafness + encephalopathy).
Emboli: Hollenhorst plaques (refractile cholesterol), fibrin-platelet (grey, elongated), calcific (white, non-shiny, near the disc).
Stroke risk is highest in the first days → urgent stroke/TIA clinic. 25% stroke at 3 years after TIA.
All: smoking, GCA symptoms (headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, PMR), pulse (AF), BP, heart murmur, ECG, ESR/CRP, FBC (platelets), glucose, lipids, U&E, carotid duplex.
Selected (young, atypical): MRI/CT, echocardiogram, 24-h ECG, CXR, homocysteine, thrombophilia, electrophoresis, TFTs, autoantibodies, syphilis, blood cultures.
Amaurosis fugax: transient monocular 'curtain' lasting minutes → treat like a TIA, urgently.
chunks.hook: Artery occlusion = a stroke of the eye. Send to the stroke team today.

cards.q: Refractile yellow cholesterol embolus in a retinal arteriole?
Triad of Susac syndrome?
cards.a: Branch retinal artery occlusions, sensorineural hearing loss, encephalopathy.

chunks.title: BRAO, CRAO & cilioretinal artery
chunks.tldr: CRAO: sudden painless near-total loss, RAPD, white retina + cherry-red spot, 'box-car' blood columns. NPL → think GCA or ophthalmic artery. A cilioretinal artery can save central vision.
points: BRAO: sudden altitudinal/sectoral field loss, ± RAPD, white oedematous retina in one sector, emboli at bifurcations, segmented ('box-car') blood. FA delayed filling. Field rarely recovers.
CRAO: severe loss (unless cilioretinal), profound RAPD.
Cherry-red spot: intact choroid seen through thin fovea, surrounded by pale swollen retina. Emboli seen in 20%.
Cilioretinal artery (~1/3 of eyes) → normal-coloured patch near the disc → central vision preserved.
Over weeks: retina clears, arteries stay thin → optic atrophy.
Rubeosis in up to ~1 in 5, earlier than CRVO (4–5 weeks) → review at 3–4 weeks then monthly; PRP ± anti-VEGF if NV.
OCT: hyper-reflective embolus at the disc. ERG: reduced b-wave (inner retina).
Cilioretinal artery occlusion: isolated (young, vasculitis), + CRVO (transient, better prognosis), + AION (GCA, very poor).
chunks.hook: Cherry-red spot in a white sea = CRAO.

cards.q: What does NPL vision in CRAO suggest?
cards.a: Giant cell arteritis or ophthalmic artery occlusion.

cards.q: ERG change in CRAO?
Cilioretinal artery occlusion + AION in an elderly patient suggests?

chunks.title: Acute treatment & after care
chunks.tldr: Retina dies within ~4–6 hours. Tried (weak evidence): ocular massage, AC paracentesis, IOP-lowering, vasodilators, carbogen, YAG embolysis. Intra-arterial rtPA: no benefit in the big trial. The main job = prevent stroke (antiplatelet, AF anticoagulation, endarterectomy if >70%).
points: Only 1/5 end ≥6/12; 2/3 worse than 6/120.

Options within 24 h: ocular massage (3-mirror lens, 10–15 s on/off, 3–5 min), AC paracentesis (27 G, 0.1–0.2 ml), apraclonidine/timolol/IV acetazolamide, sublingual isosorbide, rebreathing into a bag, carbogen, mannitol/glycerol.
YAG embolysis (0.5–2.4 mJ on a visible embolus): some good reports; vitreous/subretinal haemorrhage in ~half.
Thrombolysis: multicentre local rtPA trial showed no benefit.
After: urgent stroke clinic (95% need medication changes, 25% urgent surgery).
Antiplatelets (loading 600 mg aspirin; clopidogrel/dipyridamole) — discuss first if fibrinolysis planned.
Anticoagulate for AF. Carotid endarterectomy for symptomatic stenosis >70%.
Asymptomatic retinal embolus: higher stroke/heart risk → manage risk factors (higher bar for surgery).
chunks.hook: Can't save the retina? Save the brain.

cards.q: Carotid stenosis threshold for endarterectomy after a symptomatic retinal embolic event?
Approximate time window before irreversible retinal damage in CRAO (primate studies)?
cards.a: About 4 hours (≈6 hours postulated in humans).

chunks.title: Ocular ischaemic syndrome
chunks.tldr: >90% carotid stenosis → slow vision loss, eye pain, slow recovery after bright light. Signs: mid-peripheral blot haemorrhages, dilated (not tortuous) veins, NVI (90%), low IOP despite NVI. FA: delayed choroidal filling. 5-year mortality ~40%.
points: Older men (2:1), vascular disease, diabetes. One eye in 80%. Often missed.
Symptoms: gradual (or sudden) loss, ache (40%), bright-light amaurosis, long afterimages.

Anterior: episcleral injection, corneal oedema, flare with few cells (ischaemic pseudo-iritis), mid-dilated poorly reactive pupil, rubeosis (up to 90%), IOP may be low (poor ciliary perfusion), cataract.
Fundus: dilated but not tortuous veins, narrow arterioles, deep round/flame haemorrhages (mid-periphery), CWS, NVD > NVE, spontaneous arterial pulsation (easily induced by light pressure), CMO.
Diabetic retinopathy worse on the stenosed side.
FA: delayed choroidal filling + prolonged AV transit, vessel staining.
Carotid imaging (duplex, CTA/MRA, DSA).
Treat: steroid + mydriatic, NVG management, PRP (less reliable), anti-VEGF, carotid endarterectomy/stenting (IOP may rise after), cardiovascular work-up.
chunks.hook: OIS: NVI but soft eye, and the arteries pulse when you press.

cards.q: Key FA finding in ocular ischaemic syndrome?
cards.a: Delayed choroidal filling and prolonged arteriovenous transit time.

cards.q: How can IOP be low despite rubeosis in OIS?
cards.a: Reduced ciliary body perfusion lowers aqueous production.

chunks.title: Hypertensive retinopathy
chunks.tldr: Grades: 1 generalised arteriolar narrowing → 2 focal narrowing + AV nipping (copper wiring) → 3 haemorrhages, exudates (macular star), CWS → 4 + disc swelling (malignant).
points: Arterioles constrict (less in elderly with stiff vessels). Arteriolosclerosis → AV nipping → long-standing hypertension.
Sustained hypertension breaks the inner BRB → flame haemorrhages, oedema.
Grade 1: mild generalised narrowing.
Grade 2: focal narrowing, AV nipping, copper-wiring.
Grade 3: + dot/blot/flame haemorrhages, hard exudates (macular star), CWS.
Grade 4: + optic disc swelling = malignant hypertension (emergency).
Early markers: narrower arterioles (pre-hypertension), wider venules (glucose problems), both = preclinical cardiovascular disease.
chunks.hook: Disc swelling + hypertension = malignant → same-day medical referral.

cards.q: Which sign defines grade 4 hypertensive retinopathy?
AV nipping indicates what?

chunks.title: Hypertensive choroidopathy
chunks.tldr: Acute severe hypertension (young, pre-eclampsia): Elschnig spots (black spots with yellow halo = choroidal infarcts), Siegrist streaks (flecks along choroidal vessels), exudative RD.
points: Rare; acute hypertensive crisis in young adults.
Siegrist streaks: linear flecks along choroidal vessels = fibrinoid necrosis (malignant hypertension).
Elschnig spots: small black spots with yellow haloes = focal choroidal infarcts.
Exudative RD (can be bilateral), e.g. toxaemia of pregnancy.
Venous tortuosity also seen in chronic/pre-hypertension (many other causes too).
chunks.hook: Elschnig = Eclipse spots (dark centre, bright ring).

cards.q: Black choroidal spots with yellow haloes in malignant hypertension?

chunks.title: Sickle-cell retinopathy
chunks.tldr: HbSC = worst retinopathy. Sea fan NV at the edge of non-perfused periphery. Also salmon patches, black sunbursts, macular depression sign. No CAIs (cause sickling). Scleral buckles → anterior segment ischaemia.
points: HbS/HbC sickle under hypoxia/acidosis → vessel blockage.
SC > SS for retinopathy. Sickle trait (AS) rarely (unless diabetes etc.).
Avoid CAIs (acetazolamide/dorzolamide): promote sickling. Hyphaema → careful IOP control.
Anterior: comma-shaped conjunctival vessels, sectoral iris atrophy, rubeosis, spontaneous hyphaema.

Non-proliferative: venous tortuosity, arteriolar occlusions (incl. macular), silver-wired peripheral arterioles, disc 'sign of sickling', salmon patches (orange-red intraretinal bleeds) → schisis cavities with refractile deposits, or black sunbursts (RPE hyperplasia), macular depression sign, angioid streaks (6%).
Proliferative stages: 1 peripheral arteriolar occlusion → 2 AV anastomoses → 3 sea-fan NV (one feeder arteriole, one draining venule) → 4 VH → 5 RD (rhegmatogenous/tractional).
FA: non-perfused periphery, sea fans fill and leak (wide-field imaging).
Treat: observe (many sea fans autoinfarct) → laser/cryo to non-perfused retina (feeder ablation avoided: CNV). PPV for VH/TRD; scleral buckle → anterior segment ischaemia.
Thalassaemia: iron/siderosis + desferrioxamine → cataract, featureless iris, tortuosity, angioid streaks, pigment mottling (PXE-like).
chunks.hook: Sea fan = coral-shaped NV in the sickle-cell periphery.

cards.q: Which sickle genotype most often causes proliferative retinopathy?
Drug class to avoid in sickle patients with raised IOP?
Name of the classic proliferative lesion in sickle retinopathy?

chunks.title: Retinopathy of prematurity: zones & stages
chunks.tldr: Zones I (centred on disc, radius 2× disc–fovea), II (to nasal ora), III (temporal crescent). Stages: 1 demarcation line → 2 ridge → 3 fibrovascular proliferation → 4 partial RD (A extrafoveal, B foveal) → 5 total RD. Plus = dilated tortuous posterior vessels.
points: Premature, low birthweight, oxygen exposure (less now), illness. VEGF-driven.
Retinal vessels grow from the disc from month 4; nasal retina vascularised by 8 months, temporal by ~1 month after birth.
Zone I: circle radius = 2 × disc-to-fovea distance (with 28D lens, if you see the disc you see only zone I). Zone II: to the nasal ora. Zone III: remaining temporal crescent.
Stage 1: flat grey-white demarcation line, vessel arcading.
Stage 2: raised ridge ± tufts behind it.
Stage 3: extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation into the vitreous (peak ~35 weeks postconceptual).
Stage 4: partial RD (4A extrafoveal, 4B foveal). Stage 5: total RD.
Plus disease: dilated tortuous posterior vessels in ≥2 quadrants (+ poor pupil dilation, vitreous haze). Pre-plus.
Aggressive posterior ROP ('rush'): posterior, marked plus, ill-defined → stage 5 in days.
chunks.hook: ROP stages: Line → Ridge → Reaching (fibrovascular) → Retina lifting → Retina off.

cards.q: Stage 2 ROP is?
cards.a: A raised ridge at the demarcation line.

cards.q: Define plus disease.
cards.a: Dilated, tortuous posterior pole vessels in at least two quadrants.

chunks.title: ROP: screening & treatment
chunks.tldr: Screen babies ≤30–32 weeks or ≤1500 g, starting 4–7 weeks after birth. Treat Type 1 within 72 h: zone I any stage + plus, zone I stage 3, zone II stage 2–3 + plus. Treatment: laser or anti-VEGF (BEAT-ROP; recurrence risk).
points: Screening: indirect ophthalmoscopy (28D or 2.2 lens) + scleral depression or wide-field camera. Dilate with cyclopentolate 0.5% + phenylephrine 2.5%. Watch for apnoea.
Review every 1–3 weeks until vessels reach zone III. ~10% need treatment.
ETROP Type 1 (treat): zone I any ROP with plus; zone I stage 3; zone II stage 2 or 3 with plus.
Type 2 (watch): zone I stage 1–2 no plus; zone II stage 3 no plus.
Laser to avascular retina (replaced cryo).
Bevacizumab (BEAT-ROP): better for zone I, allows vessels to keep growing, but systemic safety unknown and late recurrence → long follow-up.
Stage 4A → PPV (~90% anatomical success). 4B/5 → poor vision.
Cicatricial ROP (~20%): straightened temporal arcades, macular/disc dragging, falciform fold, retrolental fibroplasia, RD, angle-closure glaucoma.
Long-term: myopia, squint, amblyopia.
chunks.hook: Screen the tiny (≤1500 g) and early (≤32 weeks). Type 1 → treat in 3 days.

cards.q: Screening criteria for ROP?
cards.a: ≤30–32 weeks gestation or ≤1500 g (plus sick premature babies).

cards.q: Timeframe to treat type 1 ROP?
Cicatricial ROP sign of temporal traction on the disc/macula?

chunks.title: Retinal artery macroaneurysm
chunks.tldr: Elderly hypertensive woman, one eye, saccular arteriolar bulge on a temporal arcade. Problems: exudates threatening the fovea or multi-level haemorrhage (sub-, intra-, pre-retinal). Most self-involute.
points: 75% hypertensive; dyslipidaemia. Usually solitary, 90% one eye.
Slow blur (leakage) or sudden loss (haemorrhage).
Saccular dilatation at a bifurcation or AV crossing; haemorrhage in 50%.
Blood at several levels (subretinal dark + intraretinal bright + preretinal) is a clue.
Course: chronic leak with exudate rings, bleeding, or spontaneous thrombosis/fibrosis.
FA: uniform filling, late leak. OCT for oedema.
Check BP and lipids.
Treat: observe; laser (on/around the lesion) if exudates threaten the fovea; bevacizumab; YAG hyaloidotomy for premacular blood; gas ± rtPA to displace submacular blood; PPV for persistent VH.
chunks.hook: Blood at three different depths → look for a macroaneurysm.

cards.q: Typical patient with retinal artery macroaneurysm?
Clue in haemorrhage pattern pointing to macroaneurysm?
cards.a: Blood at multiple levels (sub-, intra-, preretinal).

chunks.title: Coats disease
chunks.tldr: Young boy, one eye, leukocoria or squint. Peripheral telangiectasia + lightbulb aneurysms with massive yellow exudation → exudative RD. Must distinguish from retinoblastoma. Treat with laser (or cryo).
points: Idiopathic retinal telangiectasia, first decade. 75% male, 95% unilateral. Some have NDP somatic mutation (Norrie gene).
Leber miliary aneurysms = milder, later, localised form.
Differentials: retinoblastoma, FEVR, VHL haemangiomas, ROP.
Signs: telangiectasia + aneurysmal arteriolar dilatations (inferior/temporal periphery), intra/subretinal exudates (can collect at the macula far from the vessels), exudative RD.
Complications: rubeosis, glaucoma, uveitis, cataract, phthisis.
FA: early leakage from telangiectasia.
Younger = more aggressive.
Treat: observe mild or blind comfortable eyes; laser to leaking vessels (repeated); anti-VEGF; IVTA; cryo (more reaction); PPV for traction/total RD; enucleate painful NVG eye.
chunks.hook: Coats = Coat of yellow exudate in a boy's one eye.

cards.q: Typical demographic for Coats disease?
Main differential for leukocoria from Coats?

chunks.title: Eales, radiation, Purtscher, Valsalva, lipaemia
chunks.tldr: Eales = young Indian man, peripheral periphlebitis + NV → VH (TB link?). Radiation = DR-like changes months–years later. Purtscher = white patches after chest/long-bone trauma or pancreatitis. Valsalva = premacular bleed after straining.
points: Eales disease: young men from the Indian subcontinent, often both eyes. Stages: inflammation → occlusion → NV. Floaters/sudden loss (VH in 1/3). Periphlebitis, BRVO, peripheral non-perfusion, NV. Exclude sarcoid, TB, sickle. Treat: steroids (inflammatory), ± anti-TB, scatter laser, anti-VEGF, PPV.

Radiation retinopathy: after plaque or external beam therapy; 6 months–3 years; dose-related. Capillary occlusion, telangiectasia, MAs, oedema, exudates, CWS, haemorrhages, NV, papillopathy. Poor prognosis with papillopathy/PDR. Laser, steroids, anti-VEGF.

Purtscher retinopathy: chest compression, long-bone fracture, head injury → embolic/complement-mediated occlusion. Purtscher-like: fat/amniotic embolism, pancreatitis, pre-eclampsia, vasculitis. Sudden bilateral loss; Purtscher flecken (white patches, clear zone along vessels), peripapillary haemorrhages, CWS, disc swelling. Often limited recovery.
Valsalva retinopathy: straining (lifting, balloons) → perifoveal capillaries burst → premacular (sub-ILM/sub-hyaloid) haemorrhage. Observe or YAG membranotomy.
Lipaemia retinalis: very high triglycerides → creamy-white vessels, salmon fundus; VA usually normal.
chunks.hook: Purtscher = Pressure on the chest → white flecks.

cards.q: White retinal patches and haemorrhages in both eyes after a crush injury?
Creamy-white retinal vessels?

chunks.title: Blood disorders: leukaemia, anaemia, hyperviscosity
chunks.tldr: Leukaemia: haemorrhages, CWS, Roth spots, infiltrates ('leopard skin'), disc infiltration, orbit (kids), pseudohypopyon. Roth spots also in endocarditis, anaemia, diabetes. Hyperviscosity: huge 'sausage' veins + haemorrhages.
points: Leukaemias: ALL (kids, 90% survival), AML (older), CLL (slow), CML.
Eye more in acute leukaemia; mostly secondary (anaemia, low platelets, hyperviscosity, infection).

Fundus: flame/blot haemorrhages, CWS, Roth spots (white-centred haemorrhages), preretinal/retrohyaloid bleeds (white cell layer), peripheral NV (CML), retinal/choroidal infiltrates (mimic posterior uveitis; leopard skin in chronic), optic nerve infiltration.
Other: orbital mass (kids), iris thickening, iritis, pseudohypopyon, hyphaema, subconj haemorrhage, CN palsies.
Roth spots: leukaemia, bacterial endocarditis, diabetes, hypertension, anaemia.
Anaemia: venous tortuosity, haemorrhages/CWS/Roth spots (worse with low platelets); optic neuropathy in pernicious anaemia.
Hyperviscosity (polycythaemia, Waldenström IgM, myeloma): dilated segmented veins, haemorrhages, CRVO, conjunctival telangiectasia.
chunks.hook: Roth spot = haemorrhage with a white heart → think leukaemia or endocarditis.

cards.q: Name 3 causes of Roth spots.
cards.a: Leukaemia, bacterial endocarditis, anaemia (also diabetes, hypertension).

cards.q: Retinal sign of hyperviscosity?
cards.a: Grossly dilated, segmented ('sausage') veins with haemorrhages.
